title: Most Majestic Game
summary: Prepare a checking pawn break, test en passant, and build a mating net that makes the opponent’s promotion irrelevant.

nodes.question: Can the bishop stop both black pawns?
nodes.explanation: The study starts after the illustrated Nc6 Kxc6 sacrifice. White must create threats that do more than stop one pawn.

nodes.question: Why advance d3 instead of chasing the a-pawn?
nodes.explanation: d3 prepares c4 with check. This forces Black to resolve the pawn structure while keeping the bishop ready to control a1.

nodes.question: Must White stop promotion?
nodes.explanation: Kb7 builds a mating net against the black king. The apparent race is really about king restriction.

startContext: Begin after the knight sacrifice Nc6 Kxc6. From here, White must coordinate the bishop and pawns against two promotion threats. The selected continuations below are independently checked.
verification_scope: Three selected positions and every intermediate position in eight variations tablebase-checked; all encoded moves legal. Winning branches illustrate responses and do not enumerate every legal defense. The preceding eight-piece setup and the claim that its knight sacrifice is best are outside this tablebase check.

exercises.prompt: Why does White need d3 before c4?
exercises.answer: d3 supports c4 and covers e4. The later c4 check forces the king or pawn to respond while the bishop remains ready to control a1.

exercises.prompt: Why does a new queen fail to save Black?
exercises.answer: Kb7 controls b6 and c6. Be7 then checks along e7-d6-c5; the bishop, king and pawns cover every escape, while the queen on a1 cannot block or capture the checker.

exercises.prompt: What changes after Black captures en passant?
exercises.answer: The pawn leaves d4 and lands on c3. Bxc3 captures it and opens a diagonal to a1, stopping promotion.
